current_answer: The U.S. warning is sharper at labor-market entry: a new Census working paper finds that graduates from the most AI-exposed majors were less likely to be employed immediately after graduation and earned less in full-quarter initial jobs after ChatGPT's release. That reinforces the earlier 22- to 24-year-old hiring signal, but neither study observes firm-level AI adoption or rules out every major- or industry-specific shock. Broader U.S. job-posting research finds little distinct AI-driven decline, while task-level data show use is widespread but often shallow. The evidence points to a serious, concentrated early-career risk signal, not a proven economy-wide job-loss verdict.

catalogue_card.question: Are AI-exposed graduates already paying a price?
catalogue_card.text: A new Census study finds weaker initial employment and pay in the most AI-exposed majors. The warning is sharper; the cause is still not settled.

summary: A Census working paper finds that graduates in the most AI-exposed decile of U.S. majors were five percentage points less likely to have initial employment and had 13% lower full-quarter initial earnings after ChatGPT's release, relative to the bottom six deciles.

The result reinforces an earlier Census finding of lower hiring and employment among 22- to 24-year-olds in highly exposed industry-state cells, but both studies assign exposure rather than observe firm AI rollout.
A Federal Reserve analysis of broad U.S. job postings finds little evidence of a distinct AI-driven decline in labor demand. That does not measure graduate entry or realized hires.
Task-level U.S. survey data show AI use is widespread but shallow: at least one in five workers use it in more than 80% of occupations, while most occupations and tasks remain below half adoption.
Danish linked records still show task reorganization without detectable earnings or recorded-hours effects larger than 2% over the first two years. Outcomes differ by population, place and margin.
uncertainty: No current study can tell a reader whether their own job will be lost to AI.
The new graduate result is an exposure-based difference-in-differences study, not a firm-adoption experiment; time-varying shocks correlated with major exposure remain possible.
Job postings, hires, employment, initial earnings, hours and task use answer different questions and can move differently.
freshness_note: Updated 14 September 2026 after a new Census study of graduates, a broad job-posting cross-check and new task-adoption data. We will revise the answer when later cohorts, observed-adoption studies or stronger causal designs change it.
